title: Kick and Snare
description: Get to know the two drums that do most of the work, and the clap that often joins them.

steps.title: The two that matter most
steps.description: Strip a beat down to almost nothing and you'll usually be left with the kick and the snare. The kick is low and you feel it as much as hear it. The snare is high and sharp. They take turns: kick on 1, snare on 2, kick on 3, snare on 4. Most of what makes one groove feel different from another comes down to where these two land.

steps.title: Kick on its own
steps.description: Hit the kick by itself. In most beats, this is what you hear on beat 1.
steps.hint: The red pad labelled KCK, top left.

steps.title: Snare on its own
steps.description: Now just the snare. It usually falls on beats 2 and 4. Drummers call that the backbeat.
steps.hint: The orange pad labelled SNR, next to the kick.

steps.title: Both at once
steps.description: Hit the kick and snare together. You won't hear this on every beat, but it makes a strong accent, like at the end of a fill or on a big stop.
steps.hint: They're side by side, so two fingers will do it. Close together in time is fine.

steps.title: Kick and clap
steps.description: Lots of pop and hip-hop tracks use a clap where you'd expect a snare. Hit the kick and the clap together to hear how they sit.
steps.hint: The clap (CLP) is right under the kick, at the start of the bottom row.

steps.title: Snare and clap
steps.description: Now stack the snare and clap together. Producers do this all the time to make the backbeat sound wider and fatter.
steps.hint: SNR is on the top row and CLP on the bottom left. Hit them together.

steps.title: Find the backbeat
steps.description: In a standard beat counted "1, 2, 3, 4", where does the snare usually land?
